back: Cracking of rock caused by repeated expansion and contraction as it heats by day and cools at night; probably most effective if the rock is also damp.
The peeling of curved sheets from the surface of a rock (onion-skin weathering) by thermal stress, pressure release and chemical weathering.
Salt water enters pores and evaporates, and the crystals grow and press on the pore walls; probably the most effective desert weathering process, making honeycomb hollows (tafoni).
Thermal fracture, exfoliation, freeze–thaw (cold nights and high deserts), salt crystal growth, hydrolysis and carbonation (with moisture from dew).
The removal of loose, fine particles by the wind, lowering the surface and leaving a lag deposit (desert pavement).
Sandblasting of rock surfaces by grains in saltation; greatest in the lowest metre or so above the ground.
Traction (coarse grains roll), saltation (sand bounces and carries most of the load) and suspension (dust carried high and far).
Sand transport rate is proportional to the cube of the wind (shear) speed: doubling the speed gives eight times the movement.
A dry lake bed in Chad that is the largest source of wind-blown dust in the world; its dust is carried across the Atlantic.
